title: JavaScript
summary: Learn the language of the web from your first console.log to classes, error handling, promises and modules, with a judged exercise in every lesson.

lessons.title: Your first JavaScript program
lessons.summary: Meet JavaScript and print your first lines of text with console.log.

slides.title: What is JavaScript?
slides.text:
- The language of the **web**: every browser runs it
- With **Node.js** it also runs on your computer, outside the browser
- Used for websites, servers, desktop apps, tools and games
slides.narration:
Welcome to JavaScript, the language that powers almost every website you visit.
It started in the browser, but thanks to Node.js it now runs everywhere, including right here in Averroes Code.
In this course you will go from your very first line all the way to classes, errors and asynchronous code.

slides.title: Printing with console.log
slides.text:
`console.log(...)` prints a value and then a new line.
Text goes inside **quotes**.
slides.narration:
The first tool every JavaScript programmer learns is console dot log.
Whatever you put inside the parentheses is printed, followed by a new line.
Text must be wrapped in quotes, single or double, while numbers can be written as they are.

slides.title: Statements and semicolons
slides.text:
- Each instruction is a **statement**
- Statements run **top to bottom**
- End them with `;` (optional, but a good habit)
slides.narration:
A program is a list of statements that run one after another, from top to bottom.
We end each statement with a semicolon. JavaScript can often guess where it goes, but writing it yourself avoids surprises.

slides.title: Comments
slides.text: Comments are notes for humans. The computer ignores them.
slides.narration:
Comments let you leave notes in your code for yourself and for others.
Two slashes start a comment that lasts until the end of the line, and slash star starts a block comment that ends with star slash.

slides.title: Run it!
slides.text:
1. Type your code in the editor
2. Press **Run**
3. Read the output panel
slides.narration:
Now it is your turn. Type the code, press Run, and watch the output appear.
If something goes wrong, read the error message carefully. It usually tells you the line number where the problem is.

lessons.notes:
## Hello, JavaScript

JavaScript (JS) is the programming language of the web. Browsers run it to make pages interactive, and **Node.js** runs it on your computer so you can write tools, servers and command-line programs. Averroes Code uses Node.js to run your files.

## Printing output

```javascript
console.log('Hello, World!');
console.log(7);
console.log('Sum:', 3 + 4); // several values are separated by a space
```

- `console.log` prints its values and then a line break.
- Text (a **string**) goes inside single `'...'` or double `"..."` quotes, or backticks.
- Numbers are written without quotes.

## How a program runs

A program is a list of **statements** that run from top to bottom, one at a time. End each statement with a semicolon `;`. JavaScript has "automatic semicolon insertion", but relying on it can cause rare, confusing bugs, so most style guides write them.

## Comments

```javascript
// This is a line comment
/* This is a
   block comment */
```

Use comments to explain **why** your code does something, not to repeat what it obviously does.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Forgetting the closing quote: `console.log('Hi);` is a syntax error.
- Writing `Console.log` with a capital C. JavaScript is **case-sensitive**.
- Missing parentheses: `console.log 'Hi'` does not work.

In exercises your output is compared **exactly** with the expected output, so check spelling, spaces and punctuation.

quiz.q: Which line prints Hello?
quiz.explain: In JavaScript you print with console.log, all lowercase except the L in log.

quiz.q: What does // start?
quiz.explain: Two slashes start a comment that runs to the end of the line.

quiz.q: In what order do statements run?
quiz.explain: Statements run one after another from the top of the file to the bottom.

lessons.title: Variables and data types
lessons.summary: Store values with let and const and meet numbers, strings, booleans, null and undefined.

slides.title: Boxes with names
slides.text:
A **variable** is a named box that holds a value.
- `const` for values that never get reassigned
- `let` for values that change
slides.narration:
A variable is like a labelled box where you keep a value so you can use it later.
Use const when the box will always hold the same value, and let when you plan to change it.
You might also see the old keyword var in older code. Avoid it in new code.

slides.title: The basic types
slides.text:
- **number**: `42`, `3.14`, `-7`
- **string**: `'hello'`
- **boolean**: `true` / `false`
- **undefined**: no value yet
- **null**: "intentionally empty"
slides.code:
console.log(typeof 42);       // number
console.log(typeof 'hi');     // string
console.log(typeof true);     // boolean
console.log(typeof undefined);// undefined
slides.narration:
Every value has a type. Numbers are used for both whole numbers and decimals.
Strings hold text, booleans are true or false, and undefined means nothing has been assigned yet.
The typeof operator tells you the type of any value.

slides.title: Arithmetic
slides.text:
`+ - * /` and `%` (remainder), `**` (power).
Use `Math.floor` for whole-number division.
slides.code:
console.log(7 + 2);  // 9
console.log(7 / 2);  // 3.5
console.log(7 % 2);  // 1
console.log(2 ** 3); // 8
console.log(Math.floor(7 / 2)); // 3
slides.narration:
JavaScript does math the way you expect. Division always gives a decimal result if needed, so seven divided by two is three point five.
The percent sign gives the remainder, and two stars mean power.
To drop the decimal part, use Math dot floor.

slides.title: Strings and numbers
slides.text:
`+` with a string **joins** text.
Convert text to a number with `Number(...)`.
slides.narration:
Be careful: if one side of a plus sign is a string, JavaScript glues the values together as text.
To do real math with text you read, convert it first with Number.
Template literals use backticks and let you drop values into text with dollar sign and curly braces.

slides.title: Naming rules
slides.text:
- Start with a letter, `_` or `$`
- No spaces; use **camelCase**: `totalPrice`
- Case matters: `age` and `Age` are different
slides.narration:
Give your variables clear names. JavaScript developers use camel case, where each new word starts with a capital letter, like total price.
Remember that names are case sensitive, so age with a small a and Age with a capital A are two different variables.

lessons.notes:
## Declaring variables

```javascript
const pi = 3.14159;   // cannot be reassigned
let count = 0;        // can change
count = count + 1;
count += 1;           // shortcut, now 2
count++;              // now 3
```

Prefer `const` by default and switch to `let` only when the value must change. Avoid `var`: it has confusing scoping rules.

## Primitive types

| Type | Examples |
|------|----------|
| number | `0`, `-12`, `3.5`, `NaN`, `Infinity` |
| string | `'hi'`, `"hi"`, `` `hi ${name}` `` |
| boolean | `true`, `false` |
| undefined | a variable with no value |
| null | an intentional "nothing" |
| bigint | `123n` for huge integers |

Use `typeof value` to check a type.

## Arithmetic

`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (remainder), `**` (power). Division gives decimals: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. Use `Math.floor(7 / 2)` for `3`. Decimals can be slightly imprecise (`0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`); round with `toFixed` when printing money.

## Strings vs numbers

`'5' + 3` is `'53'` because `+` joins strings. Convert with `Number('5')` or `parseInt('5', 10)`. If conversion fails you get `NaN` ("Not a Number").

## Template literals

```javascript
const name = 'Lina';
console.log(`Hello, ${name}! 2 + 2 = ${2 + 2}`);
```

Backtick strings can contain `${expression}` placeholders and even span several lines.

quiz.q: Which keyword declares a value that is never reassigned?
quiz.explain: const creates a binding that cannot be reassigned.

quiz.q: What is '5' + 3 in JavaScript?
quiz.explain: When one side is a string, + joins the values as text.

quiz.q: What is 17 % 5?
quiz.explain: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with remainder 2.

exercise.title: Calculator
exercise.prompt:
Input: two integers `a` and `b` on one line, separated by a space (b is never 0).

Print four lines:
```
a + b = SUM
a - b = DIFFERENCE
a * b = PRODUCT
a / b = QUOTIENT
```
where QUOTIENT is the whole-number part (use `Math.trunc`). Example for `7 2`:
```
7 + 2 = 9
7 - 2 = 5
7 * 2 = 14
7 / 2 = 3
```
The starter already reads the two numbers for you; you will learn how in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Reading input
lessons.summary: Read text that the user types (standard input) and turn it into numbers and words.

slides.title: Standard input
slides.text:
Programs can read text given to them: **standard input** (stdin).
In exercises, the tests send input to your program through stdin.
slides.narration:
So far our programs only talked. Now they will listen.
Standard input, or stdin for short, is the text that is fed into your program when it starts.
The exercise tests use it to give your code different inputs and check what it prints.

slides.title: The one-line way (CommonJS)
slides.text: The classic Node.js pattern reads **all** input at once as a string:
slides.code:
const input = require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
console.log('You typed:', input);
slides.narration:
The simplest way to read everything in Node is this one line.
require loads the built-in fs module, and readFileSync with zero reads file number zero, which is standard input.
The result is one big string containing everything that was typed.

slides.title: The import way (used in exercises)
slides.text: Modern JavaScript uses `import`. It does the same job and works in every exercise:
slides.code:
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
const input = readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
slides.narration:
Modern JavaScript files use import instead of require.
It does exactly the same thing. In this course the exercises use the import form, because the checker runs your code as a modern module where require is not available.

slides.title: Splitting into lines and words
slides.text:
- `.trim()` removes extra spaces and newlines at the ends
- `.split('\n')` gives lines
- `.split(/\s+/)` gives words
- `.map(Number)` turns words into numbers
slides.narration:
Input arrives as one string, so we cut it into pieces.
Trim removes the trailing newline, split on a newline gives you the lines, and split on whitespace gives you the words.
Finally, map with Number converts each word into a real number you can do math with.

slides.title: Always convert!
slides.text: Input is **always text**. `'2' + '3'` is `'23'`, not `5`.
slides.narration:
The most common beginner bug is forgetting that input is text.
If you add two strings, you get them glued together. Convert with Number first, and your math will work.

lessons.notes:
## Reading all of standard input

In Node.js, standard input is "file descriptor 0", so you can read all of it with `readFileSync(0, 'utf8')`.

**The simple CommonJS one-liner** (works in a normal `.js` file):

```javascript
const input = require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
```

**The modern ES module form** (works in `.mjs` files and in all exercises in this course):

```javascript
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
const input = readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
```

Both give you one string with everything the user typed, including newlines. The exercise checker runs your code as a module, where `require` does not exist, so **use the `import` form in exercises**.

## Breaking input into pieces

```javascript
const lines = input.trim().split('\n');       // array of lines
const words = input.trim().split(/\s+/);       // array of words (any spaces/newlines)
const nums  = words.map(Number);                // array of numbers
const [a, b] = nums;                            // first two numbers
```

- `trim()` removes the final newline so you do not get an empty last line.
- `/\s+/` is a regular expression meaning "one or more whitespace characters".
- On Windows, lines may end with `\r\n`; `split(/\r?\n/)` handles both.

## Converting text

| Function | `'42'` | `'3.5'` | `'abc'` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Number(s)` | 42 | 3.5 | NaN |
| `parseInt(s, 10)` | 42 | 3 | NaN |
| `parseFloat(s)` | 42 | 3.5 | NaN |

## Tip

When you run a program yourself, type the input in the input box before you press Run, because the program reads it all at once.

quiz.q: What does readFileSync(0, 'utf8') read?
quiz.explain: File descriptor 0 is standard input, so it reads everything the user typed.

quiz.q: What is the type of the value returned by readFileSync(0, 'utf8')?
quiz.explain: It is one string. You must split and convert it yourself.

quiz.q: What does '4 5'.split(' ').map(Number) give?
quiz.explain: split gives the two words and map(Number) converts each one to a number.

lessons.title: Making decisions with if
lessons.summary: Compare values and choose what to do with if, else if, else and the ternary operator.

slides.title: Comparisons
slides.text:
`===` equal, `!==` not equal, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`
The result is a **boolean**.
slides.code:
console.log(5 > 3);     // true
console.log(5 === 5);   // true
console.log('5' === 5); // false
slides.narration:
Comparison operators ask a question and answer with true or false.
Always use three equal signs for equality. It checks both the value and the type, so the string five is not equal to the number five.

slides.title: if / else if / else
slides.text: Run code only when a condition is true.
slides.narration:
An if statement checks a condition. If it is true, the block in curly braces runs.
You can chain more checks with else if, and catch everything else with a final else.
Only the first matching branch runs.

slides.title: Combining conditions
slides.text:
- `&&` AND: both must be true
- `||` OR: at least one is true
- `!` NOT: flips true and false
slides.narration:
Real decisions often depend on more than one thing.
Two ampersands mean and, two vertical bars mean or, and an exclamation mark means not.

slides.title: Truthy and falsy
slides.text:
These count as **false**: `false`, `0`, `''`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`.
Everything else is **truthy**.
slides.code:
const name = '';
if (!name) console.log('No name given');
slides.narration:
In a condition, JavaScript treats some values as false even if they are not booleans.
Zero, an empty string, null, undefined and NaN are all falsy. Everything else counts as true.

slides.title: The ternary operator
slides.text:
A short if/else that produces a value:
`condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`
slides.narration:
When you just need to pick between two values, the ternary operator is handy.
Write the condition, a question mark, the value for true, a colon, and the value for false.

quiz.q: What is '5' === 5?
quiz.explain: Strict equality compares types too, and a string is not a number.

quiz.q: Which value is falsy?
quiz.explain: The number 0 is falsy. Non-empty strings and arrays are truthy.

quiz.q: What does true && false || true evaluate to?
quiz.explain: AND runs first: true && false is false; then false || true is true.

lessons.title: Loops: repeating work
lessons.summary: Repeat actions with for, while and for...of, and control loops with break and continue.

slides.title: Why loops?
slides.text: Instead of writing the same line 100 times, write it **once** and repeat it.
slides.narration:
Computers are great at doing boring things many times.
A loop repeats a block of code, so printing one to five, or one to a million, takes just a few lines.

slides.title: The for loop
slides.text:
`for (start; condition; step)`
1. run **start** once
2. check **condition**
3. run the body, then **step**, and repeat
slides.narration:
A for loop has three parts in its parentheses.
The start runs once. Before every round the condition is checked, and after every round the step runs.
When the condition becomes false, the loop stops.

slides.title: The while loop
slides.text: Repeat **while** a condition is true. Good when you do not know the number of steps.
slides.narration:
A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is true.
Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need.
Make sure something inside the loop changes, or it will run forever.

slides.title: for...of
slides.text: Visit every item of an array or every character of a string.
slides.narration:
When you want every item in a list, for of is the cleanest choice.
It hands you each item in turn, with no index to manage.

slides.title: break and continue
slides.text:
- `break` leaves the loop now
- `continue` skips to the next round
slides.narration:
Sometimes you want to skip one round, or stop early.
continue jumps straight to the next round, and break exits the loop completely.

quiz.q: How many times does for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) run?
quiz.explain: i takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3: four rounds.

quiz.q: What does continue do?
quiz.explain: continue skips the rest of the body and starts the next round.

quiz.q: Which loop is best for visiting every item of an array?
quiz.explain: for...of gives you each value directly. for...in gives keys and is meant for objects.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Package code into reusable functions with parameters, return values and arrow syntax.

slides.title: What is a function?
slides.text:
A **named, reusable** block of code.
Define it once, **call** it many times.
slides.narration:
A function is a small machine with a name. You build it once, then use it whenever you need it.
Here, greet takes a name and prints a greeting. Calling it twice gives two greetings.

slides.title: Parameters and return
slides.text:
- **Parameters** are the inputs
- `return` sends a result back and **ends** the function
slides.narration:
Parameters are the inputs listed in the parentheses.
The return keyword sends a value back to whoever called the function, and stops the function immediately.
A function without return gives back undefined.

slides.title: Arrow functions
slides.text: A shorter way to write functions, very common in modern JS.
slides.narration:
Arrow functions are a compact way to write a function.
If the body is a single expression, you can drop the braces and the return keyword, and the value is returned automatically.

slides.title: Default parameters
slides.text: Give a parameter a value to use when the caller leaves it out.
slides.narration:
Default parameters make functions friendlier.
If the caller does not pass a value, the default is used instead of undefined.

slides.title: Scope
slides.text: Variables made **inside** a function live only inside it.
slides.narration:
Scope means where a variable can be seen.
Variables declared inside a function, or inside any curly braces with let or const, disappear when that block ends.
Code inside can see variables from outside, but not the other way around.

quiz.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
quiz.explain: Without return, the result of calling a function is undefined.

quiz.q: Which is a valid arrow function that doubles x?
quiz.explain: Arrow functions use =>. A single parameter does not need parentheses.

quiz.q: function f(a, b = 10) { return a + b; } What is f(5)?
quiz.explain: b falls back to its default value 10, so 5 + 10 = 15.

exercise.title: Counting primes
exercise.prompt:
Write a function `isPrime(n)` that returns `true` when n is a prime number.

Input: one integer `n` (0 to 10000).
Print how many prime numbers are less than or equal to n.

Example: for `10` print `4` (2, 3, 5, 7).

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Store ordered lists of values, access them by index and change them with push, pop and friends.

slides.title: A list of values
slides.text:
An **array** holds many values in order.
Indexes start at **0**.
slides.code:
const colors = ['red', 'green', 'blue'];
console.log(colors[0]);     // red
console.log(colors.length); // 3
console.log(colors[colors.length - 1]); // blue
slides.narration:
An array is an ordered list. You write it with square brackets and commas between the items.
Each item has a position called an index, and counting starts at zero.
The length property tells you how many items there are.

slides.title: Adding and removing
slides.text:
- `push` / `pop`: end of the array
- `unshift` / `shift`: start of the array
slides.narration:
Arrays can grow and shrink.
Push adds to the end and pop removes from the end. Unshift and shift do the same at the start.
Notice that a const array can still be changed. Const only stops you from replacing the whole array.

slides.title: Looping over arrays
slides.text: Use `for...of` for values, or a classic `for` when you need the index.
slides.narration:
The most common thing you do with an array is visit every item.
For of gives you each value. A classic for loop with an index is useful when you also need the position.

slides.title: Searching and slicing
slides.text:
- `includes(x)`, `indexOf(x)`
- `slice(start, end)` copies a part
- `join(', ')` turns it into a string
slides.narration:
Arrays come with many helpful methods.
includes answers yes or no, indexOf gives the position or minus one, slice copies a section, and join glues the items into one string.

slides.title: Sorting
slides.text:
`sort()` sorts **as text** by default.
For numbers pass a compare function.
slides.narration:
Here is a classic trap. Sort compares items as text, so ten comes before nine.
To sort numbers, give sort a function that subtracts b from a.
Also note that sort changes the original array, so we copy it first with the spread syntax.

lessons.notes:
## Creating and reading

```javascript
const a = [10, 20, 30];
a[0];          // 10
a.length;      // 3
a.at(-1);      // 30 (last item)
a[5];          // undefined (no error!)
```

## Changing arrays

| Method | What it does | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `push(x)` | add to end | new length |
| `pop()` | remove last | removed item |
| `unshift(x)` | add to start | new length |
| `shift()` | remove first | removed item |
| `splice(i, n)` | remove n items at i | removed items |
| `reverse()` | reverse in place | the array |
| `sort(fn)` | sort in place | the array |

A `const` array can be modified; you just cannot assign a new array to the same name.

## Non-changing helpers

- `slice(start, end)` copies a part (end not included).
- `concat(other)` or `[...a, ...b]` joins arrays.
- `includes(x)`, `indexOf(x)` search.
- `join(sep)` builds a string.

## Sorting numbers correctly

```javascript
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b); // ascending
nums.sort((a, b) => b - a); // descending
```

Without a compare function, items are compared as strings.

## Useful Math helpers

`Math.max(...nums)` and `Math.min(...nums)` find the largest and smallest values. The `...` (spread) unpacks the array into separate arguments.

## Two-dimensional arrays

```javascript
const grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
grid[1][0]; // 3
```

quiz.q: const a = ['x', 'y', 'z']; What is a[1]?
quiz.explain: Indexes start at 0, so index 1 is the second item.

quiz.q: What does [10, 9, 1].sort() return?
quiz.explain: Without a compare function, items are sorted as text: "1" < "10" < "9".

quiz.q: Which method removes the last item?
quiz.explain: pop removes and returns the last item.

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.summary: Group related data with keys and values, use methods, and loop over an object.

slides.title: Key-value pairs
slides.text: An **object** groups related data under names (keys).
slides.narration:
Arrays are great for lists, but often data has named parts, like a user with a name and an age.
An object stores values under keys. You read them with a dot, or with square brackets and the key as a string.

slides.title: Changing objects
slides.text: Add, update and delete properties at any time.
slides.narration:
Objects are flexible. Assign to a new key to add it, assign to an existing key to update it, and use delete to remove one.
The in operator checks whether a key exists.

slides.title: Methods
slides.text:
A function stored in an object is a **method**.
`this` refers to the object.
slides.narration:
Objects can also hold functions, which we call methods.
Inside a method, the keyword this refers to the object the method was called on, so it can read and change its own data.

slides.title: Looping over objects
slides.text: `Object.keys`, `Object.values`, `Object.entries`
slides.narration:
To visit every property, turn the object into an array.
Object keys gives the keys, Object values gives the values, and Object entries gives pairs of both, which works nicely with for of.

slides.title: Objects as counters
slides.text: A classic pattern: count things with an object.
slides.narration:
One of the most useful patterns in programming is counting with an object.
For each word, read its current count, or zero if it is new, add one, and store it back.
For big or unusual keys, a Map is an even better tool.

lessons.notes:
## Object literals

```javascript
const book = {
  title: 'Dune',
  year: 1965,
  tags: ['sci-fi', 'classic'],
  author: { first: 'Frank', last: 'Herbert' },
};
book.author.last;   // 'Herbert'
book.tags[0];       // 'sci-fi'
```

Use dot notation for normal keys and brackets when the key is in a variable or has spaces: `book[key]`.

## Missing properties

Reading a missing key gives `undefined`. Optional chaining avoids errors on deep paths: `book.publisher?.name` is `undefined` instead of throwing.

## Methods and this

```javascript
const person = {
  name: 'Sam',
  hello() { return `Hi, I am ${this.name}`; },
};
```

Arrow functions do **not** have their own `this`, so use the method shorthand for object methods.

## Iterating

```javascript
Object.keys(book);    // ['title', 'year', 'tags', 'author']
Object.values(book);
Object.entries(book); // [['title', 'Dune'], ...]
```

Keys keep insertion order for normal string keys (integer-like keys come first, in numeric order).

## References

Objects are passed by **reference**: `const b = a;` does not copy. Changing `b.x` changes `a.x` too. Copy with `{ ...a }` (shallow) or `structuredClone(a)` (deep).

## Map

`Map` is a dedicated key-value collection that keeps insertion order for all keys and allows any type as key:

```javascript
const m = new Map();
m.set('apple', 3);
m.get('apple');   // 3
m.has('pear');    // false
```

quiz.q: const p = { x: 1 }; How do you read x?
quiz.explain: Object properties are read with a dot (or p["x"]).

quiz.q: What does Object.keys({ a: 1, b: 2 }) return?
quiz.explain: Object.keys returns an array of the key names.

quiz.q: const a = { n: 1 }; const b = a; b.n = 5; What is a.n?
quiz.explain: b and a point to the same object, so the change is visible through both.

exercise.title: Word counter
exercise.prompt:
Input: some text with words separated by spaces and/or newlines. Treat words case-insensitively (convert to lowercase).

For each different word, in order of **first appearance**, print `word: count`.

Example input `the cat and the hat` gives:
```
the: 2
cat: 1
and: 1
hat: 1
```

lessons.title: Working with strings
lessons.summary: Slice, search, transform and build text with the most useful string methods.

slides.title: Strings are sequences
slides.text:
Each character has an index, starting at 0.
Strings are **immutable**: methods return new strings.
slides.code:
const word = 'hello';
console.log(word[0]);      // h
console.log(word.length);  // 5
console.log(word.at(-1));  // o
slides.narration:
A string is a sequence of characters, and like arrays they are indexed from zero.
Strings can never be changed in place. Every method gives you a brand new string and leaves the original alone.

slides.title: Changing case and trimming
slides.text: `toUpperCase()`, `toLowerCase()`, `trim()`
slides.narration:
These are the methods you will use all the time.
Trim removes spaces from both ends, and the case methods convert the whole string to upper or lower case.
Methods can be chained, one after another.

slides.title: Searching
slides.text: `includes`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `indexOf`
slides.code:
const email = 'ada@example.com';
console.log(email.includes('@'));        // true
console.log(email.endsWith('.com'));     // true
console.log(email.indexOf('@'));         // 3
slides.narration: To find things inside a string, use includes for a simple yes or no, startsWith and endsWith to check the edges, and indexOf to get the position.

slides.title: Cutting and replacing
slides.text: `slice(start, end)`, `split(sep)`, `replaceAll(a, b)`, `repeat(n)`
slides.narration:
slice cuts out a part of a string. Negative numbers count from the end.
split breaks a string into an array, replaceAll swaps every match, and repeat copies a string several times.

slides.title: Reversing a string
slides.text: No built-in `reverse` for strings. Turn it into an array first!
slides.code:
const reversed = [...'stressed'].reverse().join('');
console.log(reversed); // desserts
slides.narration:
Strings do not have a reverse method, but arrays do.
So spread the string into an array of characters, reverse the array, and join it back together.

lessons.notes:
## Basics

```javascript
const s = 'Hello';
s.length;       // 5
s[1];           // 'e'
s.at(-1);       // 'o'
s + ' there';   // concatenation
`${s}!`;        // template literal
```

Strings are **immutable**. `s.toUpperCase()` returns a new string; `s` is unchanged.

## The most useful methods

| Method | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `toUpperCase()` | `'ab'.toUpperCase()` | `'AB'` |
| `trim()` | `' x '.trim()` | `'x'` |
| `includes(t)` | `'cat'.includes('a')` | `true` |
| `indexOf(t)` | `'cat'.indexOf('t')` | `2` |
| `slice(a, b)` | `'hello'.slice(1, 3)` | `'el'` |
| `split(sep)` | `'a,b'.split(',')` | `['a', 'b']` |
| `replaceAll(a, b)` | `'aaa'.replaceAll('a', 'b')` | `'bbb'` |
| `padStart(n, c)` | `'7'.padStart(3, '0')` | `'007'` |
| `repeat(n)` | `'-'.repeat(5)` | `'-----'` |

## Characters and codes

`'A'.charCodeAt(0)` is `65` and `String.fromCharCode(66)` is `'B'`. Useful for simple ciphers.

## Reversing and checking palindromes

```javascript
const clean = text.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '');
const isPal = clean === [...clean].reverse().join('');
```

The regular expression `/[^a-z0-9]/g` matches every character that is **not** a letter or digit, and `g` means "all of them".

## Comparing strings

`'apple' < 'banana'` compares alphabetically by character codes, so uppercase letters come before lowercase. For human-friendly sorting use `a.localeCompare(b)`.

quiz.q: What is 'banana'.slice(1, 4)?
quiz.explain: slice starts at index 1 and stops before index 4: a, n, a.

quiz.q: What does 'hi'.toUpperCase() do to the original string?
options: Nothing; it returns a new string
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable. The method returns a new string.

quiz.q: Which expression reverses the string s?
quiz.explain: Strings have no reverse method, so convert to an array, reverse, and join.

lessons.title: Higher-order functions
lessons.summary: Use map, filter, reduce, find and friends to transform arrays without manual loops.

slides.title: Functions are values
slides.text:
You can store a function in a variable and **pass it** to another function.
A function that takes or returns a function is **higher-order**.
slides.narration:
In JavaScript, functions are values, just like numbers and strings.
That means you can pass a function into another function. A function that does this is called a higher order function.
Arrays have many of them built in.

slides.title: map: transform every item
slides.text: `map` returns a **new array** with the function applied to each item.
slides.narration:
map takes a function and runs it on every item, collecting the results in a new array of the same length.
The original array is not changed.

slides.title: filter: keep some items
slides.text: `filter` keeps the items for which the function returns **true**.
slides.narration: filter is like a sieve. Your function answers true or false for each item, and only the true ones are kept.

slides.title: reduce: combine into one value
slides.text: `reduce(fn, start)` walks the array carrying an **accumulator**.
slides.narration:
reduce boils an array down to a single value.
It starts with the initial value, here zero, then for each item it calls your function with the running total and the item, and keeps the result.

slides.title: Chaining
slides.text:
Methods return arrays, so you can **chain** them.
Also: `find`, `some`, `every`, `forEach`.
slides.narration:
Because map and filter return arrays, you can chain them into a little pipeline that reads like a sentence.
find returns the first match, some asks if any item matches, and every asks if all of them do.

lessons.notes:
## Functions as values

Functions can be stored in variables, passed as arguments and returned from other functions. A function passed in is often called a **callback**.

## The big three

```javascript
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

nums.map((n) => n * 10);              // [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
nums.filter((n) => n % 2 === 1);      // [1, 3, 5]
nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);  // 15
```

All three **do not change** the original array.

The callback also receives the index: `arr.map((value, index) => ...)`.

## More helpers

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `find(fn)` | first item where fn is true, or `undefined` |
| `findIndex(fn)` | its index, or -1 |
| `some(fn)` | `true` if any item matches |
| `every(fn)` | `true` if all items match |
| `forEach(fn)` | nothing; just runs fn for each item |
| `flatMap(fn)` | map then flatten one level |

## reduce in depth

```javascript
const words = ['hi', 'hello', 'hey'];
const longest = words.reduce((best, w) => (w.length > best.length ? w : best), '');
```

Always pass the initial value (the second argument). Without it, reduce on an empty array throws an error.

## Sorting objects

```javascript
people.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age);
people.toSorted((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); // non-mutating copy
```

## When to use a loop instead

Higher-order functions are clear for transforming data. A plain `for` loop is still fine when you need to `break` early or the logic is complicated.

quiz.q: What does [1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 2) return?
quiz.explain: map applies the function to each item and returns a new array.

quiz.q: What does [5, 8, 12].filter(x => x > 6) return?
quiz.explain: filter keeps only the items for which the function returns true.

quiz.q: [1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 10) gives?
quiz.explain: Starting from 10, add 1, 2 and 3: 16.

exercise.title: Even squares
exercise.prompt:
Input: one line of integers separated by spaces.

Using `filter`, `map` and `reduce`:
- line 1: the squares of the **even** numbers, in input order, separated by spaces (print `none` if there are no even numbers)
- line 2: `sum: TOTAL` where TOTAL is the sum of those squares

Example: `1 2 3 4` gives
```
4 16
sum: 20
```

lessons.title: Destructuring, spread and JSON
lessons.summary: Unpack arrays and objects, copy and merge with spread, and convert data to and from JSON.

slides.title: Array destructuring
slides.text: Pull values out of an array into variables in one line.
slides.narration:
Destructuring is a shortcut for unpacking values.
Put variable names in square brackets on the left, and each one receives the item at that position.
It even gives you a neat one line swap.

slides.title: Object destructuring
slides.text: Pick properties by **name**. Rename and set defaults too.
slides.narration:
With objects, curly braces on the left pick properties by name.
You can give a default for missing ones, and rename a property using a colon.

slides.title: Spread and rest
slides.text: `...` **spreads** items out, or **collects** the rest.
slides.narration:
Three dots do two jobs. On the right side they spread an array or object out, which is perfect for copying and merging.
On the left side they collect the remaining items into a new array or object.

slides.title: JSON
slides.text:
**JSON** is a text format for data.
- `JSON.stringify(obj)` object to text
- `JSON.parse(text)` text to object
slides.narration:
JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. It is the most common way programs exchange data, for example over the internet.
stringify turns an object into text, and parse turns the text back into an object.

slides.title: Optional chaining and ??
slides.text:
- `a?.b` gives `undefined` instead of crashing if `a` is missing
- `x ?? 'default'` uses the default only for `null`/`undefined`
slides.code:
const order = { customer: null };
console.log(order.customer?.name);        // undefined
console.log(order.customer?.name ?? 'Guest'); // Guest
console.log(0 ?? 5, 0 || 5);              // 0 5
slides.narration:
Two more modern helpers. The question mark dot operator safely reads deep properties without crashing on null.
The double question mark gives a default value, but only when the left side is null or undefined. Unlike the or operator, it keeps a real zero.

lessons.notes:
## Destructuring

```javascript
const [first, second = 'none'] = ['a'];      // 'a', 'none'
const { title, author: { name } } = book;    // nested
function show({ name, age }) { ... }         // in parameters
```

Destructuring in parameters is very common: the function documents which properties it needs.

## Spread `...`

```javascript
const copy = [...arr];
const merged = { ...defaults, ...options };   // later keys win
Math.max(...numbers);
```

Spread makes **shallow** copies: nested objects are still shared.

## Rest `...`

```javascript
const [head, ...tail] = [1, 2, 3];      // 1, [2, 3]
const { id, ...rest } = { id: 1, a: 2 }; // 1, { a: 2 }
function sum(...nums) { ... }
```

## JSON

JSON looks like JavaScript, but keys must be in **double quotes**, and there are no functions, `undefined` or comments.

```javascript
JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: [true, null] });          // '{"a":1,"b":[true,null]}'
JSON.stringify({ a: 1 }, null, 2);                   // pretty-printed
JSON.parse('{"ok": true}').ok;                       // true
```

`JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` on invalid text, so wrap it in `try/catch` when the text comes from outside.

## ?. and ??

- `obj?.prop`, `obj?.[key]`, `fn?.()` stop and return `undefined` if the left side is `null` or `undefined`.
- `a ?? b` returns `b` only if `a` is `null` or `undefined`. `a || b` returns `b` for **any** falsy `a` (like `0` or `''`).

quiz.q: const [a, , c] = [1, 2, 3]; What is c?
quiz.explain: The empty slot skips the second item, so c gets 3.

quiz.q: What does { ...{ x: 1, y: 2 }, y: 9 } produce?
quiz.explain: Later properties override earlier ones when spreading.

quiz.q: What is 0 ?? 7?
quiz.explain: ?? only replaces null or undefined. 0 is kept.

exercise.title: Profile card from JSON
exercise.prompt:
Input: one line of JSON describing a person, with keys `name` (string), `age` (number) and optionally `skills` (array of strings).

Use `JSON.parse` and destructuring (with a default of `[]` for skills) to print:
```
NAME (AGE)
Skills: SKILL1, SKILL2, ...
```
If there are no skills print `Skills: none`.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: Model things with classes: constructors, methods, getters, inheritance and private fields.

slides.title: A blueprint for objects
slides.text:
A **class** describes how to build objects of one kind.
`new` creates an **instance**.
slides.narration:
When you need many objects of the same shape, write a class. It is a blueprint.
The constructor runs when you call new, and sets up the object's data on this.
Methods describe what every instance can do.

slides.title: Private fields
slides.text: Fields starting with `#` are **private**: only the class can touch them.
slides.narration:
Sometimes data should be protected from outside code.
A field whose name starts with a hash sign is private, and only code inside the class can read or change it.
A getter, written with get, lets outsiders read a value as if it were a normal property.

slides.title: Inheritance
slides.text:
`extends` makes a class that **builds on** another.
`super` calls the parent.
slides.narration:
A class can extend another class and inherit all its methods.
It can then override a method with its own version, and still call the parent version through super.

slides.title: Static members
slides.text: `static` belongs to the **class itself**, not to instances.
slides.narration:
Static methods are called on the class name, not on an object.
They are handy for helpers and factory functions that are related to the class but do not need an instance.

slides.title: When to use classes
slides.text:
- Data **and** behavior that belong together
- Many objects of the same kind
- Rules that must always hold (e.g. balance never negative)
slides.narration:
Classes shine when data and the actions on that data belong together, such as a bank account with deposit and withdraw.
For simple data, a plain object is often enough. Choose the simplest tool that does the job.

quiz.q: What keyword creates an instance of a class?
quiz.explain: new ClassName(...) runs the constructor and returns the new object.

quiz.q: What does a # in front of a field name mean?
quiz.explain: Fields beginning with # are private to the class.

quiz.q: In a subclass constructor, what must you call before using this?
quiz.explain: A derived class must call super() before accessing this.

exercise.title: Bank account
exercise.prompt:
Create a class `BankAccount` with a private `#balance` (starting at 0) and methods `deposit(amount)` and `withdraw(amount)`. `withdraw` must refuse to go below zero.

Input: one command per line: `deposit N` or `withdraw N` (N is a positive integer).

After each command print:
- `Balance: X` when the command succeeds
- `Insufficient funds` when a withdrawal is larger than the balance (the balance stays the same)

lessons.title: Handling errors
lessons.summary: Throw and catch errors with try, catch and finally so your programs fail gracefully.

slides.title: Things go wrong
slides.text:
- **Syntax errors**: the code cannot even start
- **Runtime errors**: something fails while running
- **Logic errors**: it runs but gives the wrong answer
slides.code:
const user = null;
console.log(user.name); // TypeError!
slides.narration:
Every programmer meets errors every day, so do not be afraid of them.
Syntax errors stop the code from starting, runtime errors happen while it runs, like reading a property of null, and logic errors give wrong answers silently.

slides.title: try and catch
slides.text: Put risky code in `try`. If it throws, `catch` runs instead of crashing.
slides.narration:
Wrap code that might fail in a try block.
If anything inside throws an error, JavaScript jumps straight to the catch block and gives you the error object.
Your program keeps running instead of crashing.

slides.title: Throwing your own errors
slides.text: Use `throw new Error(message)` when input is invalid.
slides.narration:
You can raise errors yourself with throw.
This is the right move when a function receives input it cannot handle. The caller decides how to react by catching it.

slides.title: finally
slides.text: `finally` runs **always**, error or not. Great for clean-up.
slides.narration:
A finally block runs no matter what happened, whether the try succeeded or an error was caught.
Use it for clean up work like closing a file or stopping a loading spinner.

slides.title: Custom error types
slides.text: Extend `Error` to create meaningful error classes.
slides.narration:
For bigger programs, make your own error classes by extending Error.
Then catch blocks can check with instanceof which kind of problem happened and respond differently.

quiz.q: What happens to code after a throw inside try?
options: It is skipped and catch runs
quiz.explain: Execution jumps immediately to the catch block.

quiz.q: When does finally run?
quiz.explain: finally runs whether or not an error was thrown.

quiz.q: Which is the recommended way to throw?
quiz.explain: Throwing Error objects gives a message and a stack trace.

exercise.title: Safe number parser
exercise.prompt:
Write `parseNumber(text)` that returns the number in `text`, or **throws** an `Error` with message `'TEXT' is not a number` when the trimmed text is empty or `Number(text)` is `NaN`.

Input: several lines. For each line print either `ok: N` or `error: 'TEXT' is not a number` (TEXT is the trimmed line), using try/catch.

Finally print `total: SUM` with the sum of all valid numbers.

tests.output:
ok: 5
error: 'abc' is not a number
ok: 2.5
total: 7.5

error: 'x' is not a number
total: 0

ok: -3
error: '4a' is not a number
ok: 7
total: 4

lessons.title: Asynchronous code: promises and async/await
lessons.summary: Understand the event loop, promises and async/await for work that takes time.

slides.title: Waiting without blocking
slides.text:
Some work takes time: timers, files, network.
JavaScript does **not stop and wait**. It continues and comes back later.
slides.narration:
Imagine ordering coffee. You do not stand frozen at the counter; you read the news until your name is called.
JavaScript works the same way. setTimeout schedules work for later, and the program carries on, so the lines print in the order one, two, three.

slides.title: The event loop
slides.text:
- One thread runs your code
- Finished background tasks wait in a **queue**
- When your code is idle, the **event loop** runs the next callback
slides.narration:
JavaScript runs your code on a single thread.
Slow tasks like timers happen in the background. When they finish, their callbacks wait in a queue, and the event loop runs them once the current code is done.

slides.title: Promises
slides.text:
A **Promise** is a value that will be ready later.
It is **pending**, then **fulfilled** or **rejected**.
slides.narration:
A promise is like a receipt for a result that is not ready yet.
It starts pending, then becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error.
Use then to react to success and catch to handle failure.

slides.title: async and await
slides.text: `await` pauses an **async function** until a promise settles. Code reads top to bottom again!
slides.narration:
async and await make promise code look like normal code.
Inside an async function, await waits for a promise and gives you its value.
An async function always returns a promise.

slides.title: Errors and parallel work
slides.text:
- `try/catch` works with `await`
- `Promise.all([...])` runs tasks **at the same time**
slides.narration:
Handle async errors with ordinary try and catch around await.
When tasks do not depend on each other, start them together with Promise all, which waits for all of them and keeps the results in the original order.

quiz.q: What prints first? console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); console.log('C');
quiz.explain: The timer callback waits in the queue until the current code (A and C) has finished.

quiz.q: What does an async function always return?
quiz.explain: async functions wrap their result in a Promise.

quiz.q: Which helper waits for several promises and gives results in order?
quiz.explain: Promise.all resolves with an array of results in the same order as the input.

exercise.title: Async doubler
exercise.prompt:
Write an **async** function `slowDouble(n)` that waits `n` milliseconds (use `setTimeout` inside a Promise) and then returns `n * 2`.

Input: one line of small non-negative integers (each at most 50).

Start all the calls at the same time with `Promise.all`, `await` the results, and print them in **input order** separated by spaces. Then print `done`.

Note: the numbers finish at different times, but `Promise.all` keeps the original order.

lessons.title: Modules and organizing code
lessons.summary: Split programs into files with import and export, use built-in Node modules, and meet npm.

slides.title: Why modules?
slides.text:
Big programs are split into **files** (modules).
Each module **exports** what others may use.
slides.narration:
Real programs have thousands of lines. Keeping them in one file would be a nightmare.
Modules let you split code into files, each with a clear job. A module decides what to share by exporting it, and other files import what they need.

slides.title: export
slides.text: Mark functions, classes or values with `export`.
slides.narration:
Put export in front of anything you want to share. These are called named exports.
A module can also have one default export, which is its main thing.

slides.title: import
slides.text: Pull in what you need from another file.
slides.narration:
In another file, import names inside curly braces for named exports, and without braces for the default export.
You can also import everything as one object with star as.
Paths to your own files start with dot slash.

slides.title: Built-in Node modules
slides.text:
Node ships with modules such as `fs`, `path`, `os`, `crypto`.
Prefix them with `node:` to be clear.
slides.narration:
Node comes with many built-in modules. You already used fs to read input.
Writing node colon in front of the name makes it obvious that it is a built-in module and not a package you installed.

slides.title: CommonJS vs ES modules
slides.text:
- **ES modules** (modern): `import` / `export`
- **CommonJS** (older Node): `require` / `module.exports`
- `.mjs` = ES module, `.cjs` = CommonJS
slides.narration:
You will meet two module systems. ES modules with import and export are the modern standard, used by browsers and Node.
CommonJS, with require and module exports, is older but still common in Node projects.
The file extension or the package json file decides which one Node uses.

slides.title: npm packages
slides.text:
**npm** installs code shared by others.
`npm init -y` then `npm install lodash`
slides.narration:
Finally, npm is the package manager that comes with Node. It gives you access to millions of open source packages.
Your project's dependencies are listed in package json. Choose packages carefully: fewer, well maintained dependencies are safer.

lessons.notes:
## ES modules (the standard)

```javascript
// shapes.js
export function area(w, h) { return w * h; }
export const UNIT = 'cm';
export default class Box { /* ... */ }

// app.js
import Box, { area, UNIT } from './shapes.js';
import { area as rectArea } from './shapes.js'; // rename
```

- Named exports: many per file, imported with `{ }` and the exact name.
- Default export: at most one per file, imported with any name.
- In Node, include the file extension in relative paths: `'./shapes.js'`.
- Modules run in **strict mode** and have their own scope; top-level variables are not global.
- ES modules allow top-level `await`.

## CommonJS (older Node style)

```javascript
// shapes.cjs
function area(w, h) { return w * h; }
module.exports = { area };

// app.cjs
const { area } = require('./shapes.cjs');
```

Node decides the system by extension (`.mjs` / `.cjs`) or by `"type": "module"` in `package.json`. Recent Node versions can also detect `import` syntax in plain `.js` files.

## Built-in modules

`node:fs` (files), `node:path` (file paths), `node:os`, `node:crypto`, `node:readline`, `node:http`. No installation needed.

## npm

```
npm init -y              # create package.json
npm install dayjs        # add a dependency
npm run test             # run a script from package.json
```

`node_modules/` holds installed packages; do not edit or commit it. `package-lock.json` pins exact versions so installs are repeatable.

## Organizing a project

- One module = one responsibility (e.g. `parse.js`, `format.js`).
- Keep the entry file (`main.js`) small: it imports and wires things together.
- Export pure functions so they are easy to test.

quiz.q: How do you import a default export from ./util.js?
quiz.explain: A default export is imported without curly braces and can be given any name.

quiz.q: Which is the CommonJS way to load a module?
quiz.explain: CommonJS uses require() and module.exports.

quiz.q: What file lists the npm packages a project depends on?
quiz.explain: package.json describes the project and its dependencies.

exercise.title: A slugify module
exercise.prompt:
Exercises run as a single file, so write this "module" in one file: **export** a function `slugify(text)` and use it below.

`slugify` must:
1. trim the text and convert it to lowercase
2. replace every run of characters that are not `a-z` or `0-9` with a single `-`
3. remove `-` from the start and end

Input: several lines of titles. Print the slug of each line.

Example: `  Hello, World! 2026 ` becomes `hello-world-2026`.
